item.research_question: How can high-entropy alloys be designed to achieve ultra-high strength while retaining good ductility, overcoming the limitation of near-equiatomic compositions that restrict the formation of high-volume fractions of ductile strengthening precipitates?
item.material_system: Al0.5Cr0.9FeNi2.5V0.2 (non-equiatomic, ~50 at% Ni, ~18 at% Cr, ~4 at% V)
item.processing_route: Arc-melting pure metals, casting into copper mold, solution-treating at 1200 °C for 24 h followed by water quenching, cold-rolling with 72% reduction ratio, and ageing at 600 °C or 700 °C for 1 h followed by air cooling.
item.test_conditions: Room temperature tensile testing with a nominal strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1 on dog-bone-shaped samples (gauge length 10 mm, width 3 mm, thickness 1 mm).
key_findings: Achieved an ultrahigh yield strength of 1810 MPa and ultimate tensile strength of 1905 MPa in the sample aged at 600 °C.
The strength increment relative to the solution-treated sample was >1500 MPa (>560%).
Retained good ductility with elongation of ~9–10% after achieving the maximum strength.
Formed high-content ordered L12 nanoprecipitates with a volume fraction of ~50.1% in the 600 A sample.
The L12 phases are coherent with the FCC matrix, with a lattice parameter difference of only 0.0001 nm (0.3582 nm vs 0.3583 nm).
The spinodal nanostructure contributed 1158 MPa to the yield strength, while grain boundaries contributed 212 MPa.
The total estimated yield strength increase (1524 MPa) agrees closely with the experimental result (1536 MPa).
The mean diameter of the ordered L12 precipitates was determined to be ~35 nm.
item.mechanism: The alloying strategy utilizes spinodal decomposition to create a low-misfit coherent nanostructure where the L12 nanophases resist dislocation motion by providing strong diffuse attractive obstacles to trap moving dislocations and by creating antiphase boundaries (APBs) on the slip planes when sheared by dislocations. The diffuse coherent interfaces minimize elastic strain accumulation, preventing crack initiation and maintaining ductility.
item.limitations: The authors note that the calculated strengthening contributions based on assuming spherical precipitates may underestimate the area of APBs and the strengthening effect because the actual L12 phases are irregular and interconnected. Additionally, the volume fraction calculations may not be absolutely precise.
item.future_work: The authors anticipate that this alloying strategy can offer more possibilities for the compositional design of HEAs and will open new avenues for development of ultrastrong and ductile HEAs superior to existing commercial alloys, potentially competing with traditional structural materials in rigorous service conditions.
quotes: Here we present a strategy to design ultrastrong HEAs with high-content nanoprecipitates by phase separation, which can generate a near-equiatomic matrix in situ while forming strengthening phases

This spinodal nanostructure can resist dislocation motion by providing strong diffuse attractive obstacles to trap moving dislocations and by creating APBs on the slip planes of these ordered L12 nanophases
The maximum strengthening observed in 600 A is >1500 MPa (strength increment >560%), achieving ultrahigh yield strength (YS) of 1810 MPa and ultimate tensile strength (UTS) of 1905 MPa
